speakeroldname: Right Hon. L. B. Pearson (Prime Minister):
subtopic: OBSERVANCE OF STATEHOOD DAY CEREMONIES IN WEST INDIES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I should like to draw the attention of hon. members to the holding of Statehood day ceremonies beginning today on the islands of Antigua and St. Christopher-Nevis-Anguilla, to be followed by similar ceremonies on the island of St. Lucia on March 1 and Grenada on March 3. Statehood day ceremonies will also be observed on the islands of St. Vincent and Dominica on dates to be announced later.
These Statehood day ceremonies mark the assumption of a new constitutional status of association with Britain based on agreements negotiated by the six commonwealth Caribbean islands and the British government. The new constitutions provide for full internal self government while Britain remains responsible for defence and external relations, apart from trade, aid and migration.
The new constitutions of the West Indian Associated States will enable them to play a full role in the development of the new and closer relationship between Canada and all the Commonwealth Caribbean countries.
I know hon. members will join me in extending sincere good wishes for the future to the West Indies Associated States as they assume their new status.

speakeroldname: Right Hon. J. G. Diefenbaker (Leader of the Opposition):
subtopic: OBSERVANCE OF STATEHOOD DAY CEREMONIES IN WEST INDIES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, this is one occasion when we all can join in complete agreement with what has taken place among the states in the Caribbean, and in paying tribute not only to the residents of the various areas and islands but also to the beneficent efforts of Great Britain in providing these people with a form of government by which they are ensured a civil service system to maintain and carry out the democratic principle.
I certainly join with the right hon. Prime Minister in offering congratulations not only to these several countries and their leaders
but also to a commonwealth which makes possible the development and expansion of those countries which come under its sway, so that when the days of colonialism are over these countries may take their place as part and parcel, either directly or indirectly, of the commonwealth as a whole.

subtopic: OBSERVANCE OF STATEHOOD DAY CEREMONIES IN WEST INDIES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the members of this party wish to join with the right hon. Prime Minister and the right hon. Leader of the Opposition in extending our congratulations to the West Indies Associated States on this very historic occasion. I am certain that when the history of our era is written one of the great triumphs of the United Kingdom will be recorded as the manner in which during the past 25 years it has divested itself of an empire and created a commonwealth of free nations freely associated together. This is a transition which has come about peacefully and with a very high degree of statesmanship.
Now that the constitutions of the West Indies Associated States are set up, these states will have many economic and political problems. I should like to make the appeal I have made before in this house, and express the hope that Canada will take a much greater interest in the Caribbean area. The people there are close to us; many of them speak either English or French. We are admirably suited, both by language and common association in the commonwealth, to play an important role in their economic, cultural and social development. I hope that Canadians will take this responsibility seriously and play an ever more important role in the development of that particular area of the world.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the members of our group join with the Prime Minister (Mr. Pearson) and the spokesmen of the various parties in the house to say how happy we are to see that the West Indies Associated States had the courage to direct their own affairs. In this age of progress, colonialism is gradually disappearing. We are happy to see also that while moving ahead those people are keeping alive the democratic spirit of the free world.

West Indies Associated States Mr. Speaker, since the importance and influence of those associated states throughout the world are unquestionably growing, it is desirable that Canada should maintain relations with those states to be able, if need be, to give them help or ask them for help. We can also assure them of our friendship particularly in view of the present conditions in the world. speechtext: for leave to introduce Bill No. C-272, to amend the British North America Act, 1867 (duration of House of Commons).

subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING PROVISIONS CONCERNING ELECTIONS
speechtext: Explain.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING PROVISIONS CONCERNING ELECTIONS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, this bill is a personal centennial project designed to provoke discussion in depth of the state of parliamentary and responsible government in 1967. To achieve its aim of restoring the independence of private members of parliament, the bill has four features. It would abolish the royal power of dissolution and substitute fixed dates of elections, subject to the right of the House of Commons itself and not the Prime Minister to determine a different and earlier date.
Second, defeat of a government proposal would lead to an election only if the house itself so determined by resolution.
A third and concomitant provision of the bill is that the House of Commons would have continuous legal existence, and in case of international or national crises parliament could be called into session even during an election campaign.
Finally, parliament would be required to make financial provision for the administration during an election period, and governor general's warrants would be abolished. The bill would apply to the twenty eighth and suDsequent parliaments.
Motion agreed to and bill read the first time.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I wish to introduce this bill entitled "An act respecting the right of privacy". Mr. Justice Brandeis has referred to the right of privacy as the right most valued by civilized men. Several outstanding jurists in Canada share the same opinion. It is advisable to protect that right adequately and to stop the various forms of invasion of privacy. Recent unfortunate events in British Columbia have focussed public attention on this question.
I am introducing this bill at the request of certain members of our party in British Columbia and certain trade union members in that province. After reading of the consideration that is being given to this question in other countries I have spent a good deal of my spare time studying this subject.
The purpose of this bill is to provide that wire tapping and eavesdropping be prohibited except in cases of the administration of justice and the security of the state.

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I beg for leave, under standing order 26, seconded by the hon. member for Megantic (Mr. Langlois), to move the adjournment of the house for the purpose of discussing a definite matter of urgent public importance, namely, the situation now prevailing on the St. Lawrence river. Mr. Speaker, I am prepared to argue that the matter is of urgent public importance, and that it should be discussed today.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
subtopic: SHIPPING
subsubtopic: ICEBREAKING OPERATIONS IN ST. LAWRENCE -MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 26
speechtext: The hon. member for Lapointe may make his comments on the urgency of discussing this question today.

subtopic: SHIPPING
subsubtopic: ICEBREAKING OPERATIONS IN ST. LAWRENCE -MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 26
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, there are two reasons for the urgency of the debate. First, you have the safety of many sailors now on board ice-bound ships; I feel we must take immediate action, for tomorrow may be too late.

I simply wish to quote a representative of the Danish shipping company, owner of three of the ships at present ice-bound near Montreal. He said:

[DOT]-he was more concerned with the question of safety to his ships than with the money lost digging the vessels out-[DOT]
The spokesman said the men aboard the Danish freighters are starting to worry about their predicament.

Mr. Speaker, the matter is urgent precisely because of the security of the people on board the ships that are trapped by the ice since Thursday, people who at this very moment wonder what lies in store for them in the next few hours.
The same spokesman added, and I quote:

"There's no telling what hundreds of tons of ice can do. Ships stuck in a moving jam helplessly smash into whatever stands in the way."

Mr. Speaker, there is the question of the immediate security of these men who are trapped on the ships.
Another point may help to prove the urgency of discussing this problem today: if no decision is made immediately, the whole economic activity of a Canadian region, namely that of Montreal, will be seriously affected. In this connection I should like to point out what a Montreal spokesman for the National Harbours Board said, and I quote:

"It only stands to reason that If ships can't get in and out of here in the winter, they're going to stop coming," he said.

Mr. Speaker, that spokesman is not now referring only to the three ice-bound Danish ships but also to the three ice-bound Russian ships.
And this Montreal spokesman of the National Harbours Board further stated:

"Many shipping lines have already hinted that their ocean going vessels won't go further than Halifax or Saint John, New Brunswick. Thousands of dollars are lost each day their ships are immobilized."

In addition, the spokesman of the Danish shipping company, one of the companies
February 27, 1967



which most contributed to promote winter navigation on the St. Lawrence, stated:

He added that ship owners who have spent millions of dollars building steel reinforced hulls to trade here during the winter expect co-operation in keeping the St. Lawrence navigable.

Therefore, Mr. Speaker, shipping companies are now beginning to talk about not sending their ships and ocean-going vessels as far as Montreal harbour, because the Department of Transport is not doing anything to assist those ships, as indicated by the statements of the authorities I have just quoted.
Therefore, there are two reasons which militate for an emergency debate today. The first consideration is the safety of the many sailors confined on board their ship in extremely dangerous circumstances, according to the spokesman for the shippers.
Second, no announcement has been made, nor has any decision been taken in this regard; shippers may well decide not to use the St. Lawrence river any more, which would cause the economic areas of Montreal, Sorel, Trois-Rivieres and Quebec to suffer serious losses.
Mr. Speaker, I believe the safety of the men and the economy of the above-mentioned areas are reason enough to consider this a matter of great urgency. We have no right to endanger the lives of these men courageously trying to get through in order to develop the economy of the St. Lawrence area, year after year, without the co-operation of the government. I feel the matter is urgent, because human lives are at stake.
[DOT] (3:00 p.m.)

subtopic: SHIPPING
subsubtopic: ICEBREAKING OPERATIONS IN ST. LAWRENCE -MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 26
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I do not always agree with the political opinions of the hon. member for Lapointe (Mr. Gregoire) but I do agree with him that when ships are caught in the ice we should get them out. I am aware of the fact that he has raised this subject in the past, but I would like to point out that not only is the question of security involved but also winter trade between Canada and other countries whose ships are now trapped in the ice of the St. Lawrence.
The ship owners have indicated that it is the responsibility of the federal government to take some action. If the federal government does not want to assume this responsibility it should so inform the harbours board,
St. Lawrence Shipping which would then have to act accordingly. Under present circumstances there is a security problem involving these three ships which are trapped in the ice and cannot budge, and a very dangerous situation might arise depending which way thousands and thousands of tons of ice might move.
The point I want to make, Mr. Speaker, is that the government has permitted its icebreaker to move down the St. Lawrence river, leaving these three ships in this critical situation. We are not very happy at the fact that the government or someone has issued the order instructing the icebreakers to move downriver, because it does leave the crews of these vessels exposed to a hazardous situation. We have had enough incidents to date on the waterways in and around Canada, and if we take the precaution of preventing another then this will be one less for the record.
I for one agree on this occasion with the hon. member for Lapointe, and I think we should do something, if possible, to free these ships from the ice.
Hon. John N. Turner (Minister without
Portfolio): Mr. Speaker, I should like to speak to this motion on behalf of the Minister of Transport (Mr. Pickersgill), and I address my remarks to the urgency of debate. I concede that conditions in the St. Lawrence river channel have been extremely difficult for some weeks, with repeated jams both in Montreal harbour and lower down the channel. It is true that today the jam does extend from Sorel down to the bridge at Trois-Rivieres. Montreal harbour has also been jammed. However, I might say that the ice control structure is in operation and working effectively, and the water level in the port of Montreal has dropped to a point where I am now advised there is no danger to the Expo site.

St. Lawrence Shipping

subtopic: PROVISION FOR ESTABLISHMENT OF APPEAL BOARD
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, having been a member of the standing committee on immigration and having had the privilege to serve as parliamentary secretary to two ministers of citizenship and immigration, naturally I am interested in this important and absorbing subject. For years I have given attention to problems and questions in respect of the admission to Canada of prospective immigrants.
In the nine-year period during which I have had the honour to represent the constituency of Fort William, I have consistently maintained that Canada's immigration policies were out of date. In 1962 barely 72,000 immigrants were admitted and we lost nearly as many persons to the United States. That was approximately the situation when in
February 27, 1967	COMMONS
April, 1963 the present government took office. At that time a start was immediately made to give substance to the statement in the speech from the throne which promised that the government would give attention to the need to encourage immigration.
Subsequently, under the energetic direction of dedicated ministers, the mists which obscured the operations of the immigration services in the past began to clear away. Now, under the dynamic leadership of the present minister, we are assured of an immigration policy worthy of this great nation which has the greatest open spaces to be found anywhere in the world. I am sure every hon. member will agree that positive factors have replaced negative motivations with regard to Canadian immigration.
The white paper, which took two years of intensive study involving many changes, has been the subject of scrutiny by the press and the public in general. It has been before the joint committee of the Senate and the House of Commons on immigration. This committee has recently heard views expressed by many interested individuals and organizations both in Ottawa and Toronto, and spent three days last week in Montreal. It is about the meetings held in Montreal that I wish to speak briefly. Excellent briefs were presented to the committee. During the time that the committee was discussing a brief submitted by the United Council for Human Rights, dealing with the immigration appeal board, the hon. member for Parkdale moved that the house leader be asked to hold clause 1 of the bill to enable members to express their views at the Montreal hearings. This is precisely the reason I wish to participate in the final stage of debate on this important bill.
First of all, I should like to join those who have preceded me in extending sincere congratulations to the minister for introducing this legislation which can be likened to the appointment of an ombudsman who cuts through red tape to fight the ordinary citizen's battle when he gets embroiled in difficulties with government departments. During the past four years many cases have come to light in which immigrants have had trouble with the law and have been confined to jail for long periods without knowing their rights. Most immigrants do not know the laws of this country and if they run into trouble with the immigration department they are almost helpless. The immigration appeal board should be the answer to any unreasonable conditions or demands made by officers of
Establishment of Immigration Appeal Board the immigration department in cases of detentions, refusals to grant extensions of temporary permits, and requests for change from one non-immigrant status to another nonimmigrant status.
[DOT] (3:40 p.m.)
The brief of the United Council for Human Rights stressed the particular concern about the exclusion from the board's jurisdiction of the power to examine into and determine the justification for decisions, based on criminal intelligence reports which are undisclosed, to refuse stay of deportation. An important point of their submission was to the effect that the powers of the appeal board with respect to appeals from refusals to approve sponsorship applications made by Canadian citizens were altogether too restrictive. I agree with their contention and I also urge the minister that appeals from the rejection of sponsorship applications made by any landed immigrant be allowed.
The Catholic immigrant services of Canada made a powerful appeal to the committee on behalf of sponsorship under the auspices of accepted voluntary organizations. The history of immigration to Canada to date has proven the contribution to Canada and to the immigrant that this organization has made in the past. Their submission made it clear that this organization is prepared to continue to work on a partnership basis with the department. Their feeling is that there should be some provision for continued co-sponsorship arrangements with such organizations.
The general feeling expressed by several witnesses was that the white paper proposes an increase of unsponsored immigrants and a decrease of sponsored immigrants. It suggests that sponsored immigrants generally are unskilled and their educational level is not according to the desired standard. The fact is that the sponsored immigrant adapts very easily under the guidance of his sponsor who, in the great majority of cases, becomes his benevolent protector. As everyone knows, the family ties of most European people are very close and a nephew or even a cousin and certainly adult children or brothers and sisters are considered as being part of the family, even if they are married. This is an important consideration.
With regard to educational standards required for admission, this is considered by nearly everyone to be the most decisive deterrent to attracting the number of people we should be looking for to populate our vast country. Regardless of the number of years
13504	COMMONS
Establishment of Immigration Appeal Board an immigrant may have spent at school, the advent of automation makes it necessary to train and retrain several times in a lifetime, and that applies equally to the Canadian born as well as to newcomers.
In this regard I wish to refer to the excellent presentation made on behalf of the government of Manitoba by Hon. Sydney Spivac, Minister of Industry and Commerce, in which he pointed out that the requirements of that province are in the order of 3,500 unskilled immigrants yearly up to a maximum of 10,000 in the next few years. He contended, and I agree, that certain aspects of the policy outlined in the white paper, while claiming to be non-discriminatory in terms of geography and race, do in fact discriminate against the kind of people his province needs today to enable its economy to expand and grow. Rigid admission standards based primarily on education are unrealistic and do not meet the needs of the economy. They are discriminatory rather than expan-sionistic.
The Mining Association of Canada, in a brief presented to the committee, described the difficulties which many mining companies have experienced during the past two years in recruiting in Canada a labour force adequate to maintain their productive capacity, and suggested that the mining industry will continue to suffer from shortages of suitable manpower unless greater recourse is made to immigration and the educational requirements for unsponsored immigrants are modified.
I have a letter from the chief engineer of Canadian National Railways addressed to Mr. R. F. Welch, president of R. F. Welch Limited of Port Arthur, Ontario, the firm charged with the responsibility of recruiting manpower for building and maintenance of tracks, which I wish to put on record. It reads as follows:
Canadian National Railways has experienced serious difficulty during 1966 in securing the necessary labour for major track maintenance programs and new track construction.
There is every indication that the shortage of track labour will become even more serious for the 1967 working season. Next summer, in addition to the major track programs to be carried out on existing lines, track laying will be required on five new branch lines. I understand you have had some preliminary conversations and exchange of correspondence, with the regional engineers on the great lakes, prairie and mountain regions, regarding manpower supply.
You are hereby authorized to recruit eight hundred (800) men for work on track maintenance and construction gangs on these regions of C.N.

DEBATES	February 27, 1967
lines during the 1967 working season. Three hundred (300) of these men can be guaranteed twelve months' employment, but the balance of five hundred (500) will be required for the six months' working season only-May to October.
Please keep me advised of your progress in securing these men.
The letter is signed by A. V. Johnston, chief engineer of the engineering department of Canadian National Railways, Montreal.
I do not wish to take the time to refer to a dozen other briefs and submissions made by responsible individuals and organizations, nearly all of them pointing to the fact that the number of years in school or I.Q. tests or academic degrees do not always spell brilliance or even brightness in assessing the desirability of prospective immigrants. It is not even ability that determines performance. I venture to say that dedication, perseverance or just plain good habits and determination are other dimensions to be considered in gauging a person's effectiveness in any job.
I should also like to say a word in favour of establishing some ways and means to enable immigrants from the Ukraine to join their relatives and friends in Canada. I realize that it is not the government's fault we are not getting immigrants from eastern Europe. Nevertheless, I believe that an approach should be made to the U.S.S.R. for a review of their attitude toward a humane immigration policy which would go a long way to establishing greater and more effective friendly relations between our two countries.
[DOT] (3:50 p.m.)

speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, in rising to take part in this debate let me first of all deal with a problem created last week when the committee on immigration held a meeting in the city of Montreal at the same time the House of Commons was dealing with the bill now before us. I think that the circumstances which prevailed point up more clearly than anything else the lack of planning on the government benches with regard to the preparation of the work of the House of Commons. We have heard the Prime Minister and other cabinet members pay lip service to the role committees can play in the preparation of legislation and in helping to make the work of the House of Commons proceed in a more orderly and effective manner. Not only in the immigration committee but in other committees of the house we have seen the spectacle of the House of Commons dealing with legislation at the same time as the appropriate committee was sitting in some part of the parliament buildings or outside the
February 27, 1967	COMMONS
capital of our nation. To my mind this points us the real need of hon. members opposite, particularly those charged with the order of business that is brought before the house, to take another look at the way in which they have discharged their responsibilities in this regard. Indeed, I cannot help but feel that this was an affront to the members of the committee and parliament itself and as such should be noted in the record at this time.
Every member of the committee had to make a choice whether to stay here or go to Montreal. Many of us went to Montreal because we thought we should hear from the people who had representations to make before we came back to the House of Commons to consider the legislation that was before the house. Now we are presented with an accomplished fact; everything in the bill has been dealt with except clause 1. The hon. member for Fort William indicated that the hon. member for Parkdale had moved that only clause 1 be held in abeyance. I do not think this is quite correct. I think the hon. member for Parkdale indicated that consideration of this bill should be delayed until we had heard the representations to be made to us. I wanted to set the record straight in that regard.
The situation thus created resulted in our committee sitting in Montreal almost without any representation from the New Democratic Party. Apparently they thought it was more important to be here in the House of Commons. This points up the whole question of which is more important and where the duty of a member lies. This confused situation exists when there is inadequate planning in respect of the business of the house.
I know that Bill C-220 does not deal with the whole sphere of immigration matters but the hon. member for Fort William said something about the white paper and perhaps at this time, Mr. Chairman, you would allow me to say a word or two about it. I do not wish to deal with this question at any length. The hon. member for Fort William referred to the fact that there had been a two-year study of immigration. In view of the fact that for two years the minister considered this question, when I look at the shortcomings of the white paper, which has failed to recognize the need for unskilled and semi-skilled people in this country and has created a number of other discriminations in regard to families and so on, I cannot help but wonder what consideration was given to this matter during those two years.
Establishment of Immigration Appeal Board
I should like to make one suggestion to the minister with regard to some of the hearings that have so far been held. I urge the minister to consider the urgent need of an immigration officer and office in Beirut, Lebanon. There is a real need for opening an office there. I should like the minister to give this matter his careful and considerate attention.
In considering the legislation before us I am very glad that the hon. members who were here were able to bring forward the amendment which has made it possible for a person making an appeal to have laid before him the information forming the basis upon which deportation was decided. This will give him an opportunity to prepare his defence and lay out his case in a more orderly manner than has been the case in the past. Without saying anything further in that regard, Mr. Chairman, I shall conclude my remarks.

Mr. Chairman, in beginning my remarks on clause 1 of Bill C-220 I hasten to thank the Minister of Manpower and Immigration for reopening this clause. This gives the members of the special committee on immigration, who were doing their duty in Montreal hearing briefs from important regional and national organizations on Canadian immigration policies as outlined in the white paper, an opportunity to express their views on this question. It was just and courageous of the minister to grant the members of our committee the opportunity to exercise our right, state our views today and make them known to the committee of the whole. We are glad to have this opportunity to place before the committee of the whole the representations put before us when hearing briefs in Toronto, Ottawa and Montreal.
May I say at the outset that I was the one responsible for the action taken by the minister, having moved in Montreal a motion to inform the house leader that the members of the Committee who were in Montreal should be able to make known to the committee of the whole the views of these important national organizations, especially the views of the United Council for Human Rights which represents no less than 24 very important organizations in the greatest city of Canada.
The United Council for Human Rights is composed of the Quebec Federation of Labour, the Confederation of National Trade Unions, the Canadian Jewish Congress, the United Nations Association in Canada, the Office des Oeuvres de L'Archeveche de
13506	COMMONS DEBATES	February 27, 1967
Establishment of Immigration Appeal Board Montreal, and many other important organizations. I was shocked, and so were the members of the committee, I believe, to hear some of the grievances that were expressed. These grievances are outlined in the brief presented to us. I do not want to take the time of the committee of the whole to read them but they are grievances which merit the attention of the house and especially of the minister. They cry out for the recognition of human rights, because in dealing with matters of immigration we are concerned with the dignity of the human person.
I also wish to answer some of the remarks that were made last Thursday in the committee of the whole. It was said on that occasion that the members of the immigration committee had no right to express the views that we did in Montreal. One of the reasons given was that Bill C-220 has nothing to do with the white paper. May I draw to your attention, Mr. Chairman, that the new immigration appeal board is mentioned specifically in the white paper in sections 88, 90 and 92. The new immigration appeal board and matters connected with it are also mentioned in the second Sedgwick report on immigration at pages 6 to 10. I believe this is proof enough that the immigration appeal board was a matter for study and consideration by our committee. This has been accepted by the chairman. I believe that these remarks negate what was said last Thursday night, namely, that we had no right to ask the committee of the whole to hear our views about the immigration appeal board.
[DOT] (4:00 p.m.)
The briefs which were presented in Toronto, Ottawa and Montreal pointed out the necessity of extending the classes of relatives that can be sponsored by Canadian citizens and landed immigrants. This point is dealt with under clause 17 of the bill and I understand that several amendments were proposed to change it and the related clauses.
I understand the difficulty of the minister in trying to satisfy every point of view. However, I believe it is my duty, representing as I do the constituency of Parkdale almost 50 per cent of which is composed of people of ethnic origins other than French and Anglo-Saxon, to express the views of my constituents. I hear from them about many cases dealing with immigration problems which call for humanitarian, moral and compassionate action. I also receive representations on the same subject from all across Canada and they

are also based on humanitarian and compassionate grounds. Unfortunately, owing to the way in which the department has been run so far, it has been very difficult to obtain a favourable decision in most of these cases in which appeals have been made on compassionate and moral grounds. For this reason I appreciate the fact that amendments have been made to certain clauses allowing for compassionate grounds to be taken into account in the review of appeals.
However, there are other recommendations which have been made in the briefs from important national organizations. One of them is that the classes of relatives which can be sponsored should be extended. According to the white paper on Canadian immigration policy, a Canadian citizen can only sponsor up to an unmarried niece or nephew under 21 years of age. Most of the representations made to me, and I believe to other members of the house, have asked for an extension of the class of relatives that can be sponsored to include first and second cousins. In some cases, requests have been made to extend the class of sponsorable relatives to next of kin.
The reason for these requests is that many Canadian citizens do not have close relatives in the old country but wish to bring their next of kin who might be their fourth or fifth cousin. I believe that the Canadian government should grant Canadian citizens the right to appeal to the board asking for an extension of the classes of relatives specified in the regulations designated by the governor in council.
I make these remarks in the presence of the Minister of Manpower and Immigration because I feel it is my duty as a member of parliament to voice the wishes of the people whom I represent in this house. I believe in government of the people, for the people and by the people. We are here to legislate for the people. The people want these changes for which they have been asking for the past four years. If we turn a deaf ear to their demands we will be acting in a rather contemptuous manner. I wish to stress how important it is to listen to the requests of Canadian citizens. I am happy to have been granted the opportunity this afternoon to make these representations in the committee of the whole.
May I also express words of appreciation for the arduous task which the minister is performing. I realize that he has made more progress in immigration matters than any other immigration minister in Canadian history and I want to pay him a tribute for his efforts. I also wish to urge him to continue his

work and to take our remarks into consideration.

Mr. Chairman, I want to comment briefly on the point that has been discussed this afternoon and I can assure members of the committee I shall stick to the principle of the bill. A comment has been made with reference to an incident that took place in the committee on immigration last Thursday in the city of Montreal. I must admit I was somewhat disappointed and frustrated at having to be away from the house when this important bill to set up an appeal board was under discussion. At the same time I felt that the benefit of attending the committee hearings in Montreal would in the long run be of some useful purpose in gaining a wider understanding of the problems of the very difficult field of immigration.
I must confess too that I thought it might have been a deliberate government stratagem to have the members of the house most directly interested in immigration matters elsewhere at the time such an important item as Bill No. C-220 was before the committee of the whole. Obviously, Mr. Chairman, judging from the comments of the hon. member for Parkdale and the chairman of the committee, the hon. member for Cartier, there was no deliberate stratagem. It was just lack of good planning and management that the two activities relating to immigration took place simultaneously.
The new approach to the functions of house committees has been heralded by the government as an improvement in the management of the growing complexities of the business of this house. That could be, but unless there is
February 27, 1967	COMMONS
overall co-ordination to avoid the situation which confronted us last week this approach, rather than assisting and facilitating the business of the house, is going to create a further log jam. As a matter of fact, this debate was held over from last Thursday because of the criticism that had arisen in the committee. We have been proceeding now for an hour or so to debate matters that could have been resolved had there been proper co-ordination. I feel that the present operation of the committee system instead of facilitating the business is confusing and aggravating. There are so many committees sitting that it is quite impossible for members to give attention to their respective committee responsibilities.
At the same time, Mr. Chairman, I can sympathize with the hon. member for Park-dale in his concern because the brief presented to the committee in Montreal last Friday by the United Council for Human Rights pertained specifically to the legislation before the house. On looking at Hansard to review the debate which took place last week in the absence of the members of the committee I find that the United Council for Human Rights dealt precisely with one of the points which were raised with considerable force and skill by the hon. member for Carleton. That was the matter of the reference of security cases to the appeal board. The suggestion of the United Council for Human Rights was that we might consider security cases under the two heads of criminality and subversion and cases in the first category might be referred to the appeal board. I know that the minister put up a strong argument that in cases of subversion sources of information are dried up if they come before an appeal board and are discussed publicly.
This question was discussed in the committee last week and the United Council for Human Rights was aware of this difficulty. At the same time it saw no need for such hush-hush procedures in cases involving security based on criminality. In view of the debate last week this is all water that has gone under the bridge. Clause by clause consideration of the bill has already taken place. Some excellent amendments put forward by hon. members were acceded to and they do improve the bill. At this state an opportunity is merely being provided on clause 1 to make general statements, and I thought it was incumbent upon me to add my voice to those of others who have protested against the lack of co-ordination and the further confusion of our business which has resulted from the failure

Bill No. C-220 to establish an appeal board is an important bill. As I recall, there have been no changes in immigration policy since January, 1963, when very dynamic leadership was given to the immigration department by my colleague the hon. member for Carleton, and I am delighted to see that he has been most active in the course of the committee deliberations.
Perhaps I should add one other comment We had an interesting presentation on Friday last, by a very fine group representing the West Indies, I believe, and they wound up their presentation with that well known French adage, "Plus ga change, plus c'est la mane chose". That was their summation of the white paper as it stands. I am sure that had they looked at the original form of the bill to establish the appeal board they would have made the same comment. As I say, some worth-while amendments have been made, which is an indication of what can be done when opposition and government work together to achieve beneficial results in the most important field of immigration.
I am not going to press the brief of the Manitoba government because I might be accused of being prejudiced in this regard. I am sure that the minister will read it with a great deal of edification because I think it points to one of the great weaknesses in the white paper, namely, that it is oriented toward our urban, industrial, metropolitan communities. The fact is that in certain parts of Canada, so far as manpower needs on our frontier are concerned, there is still much to be taken care of by a dynamic immigration policy. However, this is another matter which lies in the future. We shall be considering immigration in its broad perspective in due course and we will have many more comments to make at that time.

subtopic: MEASURE TO RELIEVE LOSS OR HARDSHIP RESULTING FROM INTERRUPTION OF SERVICES

speechtext:
Hon. L. T. Pennell (for the Minister of
Justice) moved the second reading of Bill No. S-55, to provide relief in certain cases against loss or hardship suffered as a result of interruptions of normal postal services.
He said: Mr. Speaker, some federal enactments impose a time requirement or period of limitation within which something must be done. If a person fails to comply with such a time requirement or period of limitation, other than by his own choice, he may suffer loss or hardship. One example of a time requirement or period of limitation of that kind is found in section 28 of the Patent Act, which imposes a time requirement with respect to the filing of an application for a patent for an invention. If the time requirement is not complied with, no patent can issue for the invention and the invention will fall into the public domain.
It is known that a number of persons missed time limits of one kind or another under the Patent Act and the Trade Marks Act as a result of the postal strike in 1965. Although it is likely that all cases of time limits missed under industrial property legislation as a result of that strike have by now come to the government's attention, there is, of course, no way of being certain that that is

February 27. 1967	COMMONS DEBATES	13511
so or of knowing whether there are cases that have not come to our attention of time limits missed under other federal enactments. Moreover, it is not possible to foresee under what federal enactments time limits may be missed as a result of any future interruption of normal postal services.
The purpose of this bill is, therefore, to provide a way in which relief may be obtained by persons who, because of an interruption of normal postal services, suffer loss or hardship as a result of failing to comply with a time requirement or period of limitation contained in any law of Canada. This bill will apply not only to the interruption of normal postal services caused by the postal strike in 1965, but also to any subsequent local or national interruption of normal postal services however caused. A flood or other local disaster is an example of something that might cause a local interruption of normal postal services.
The bill provides that a person who wishes to obtain relief must apply to a judge of the Exchequer Court of Canada. He must also give 14 days notice of the application to the deputy attorney general of Canada and to any other person who he has reason to believe may be affected by any order that may be made pursuant to clause 3 of the bill. In order to ensure as far as possible that the application for relief will come to the attention of all interested third parties, clause 4 provides that the judge may direct the applicant to give public notice of the hearing of the application. By providing in the bill that notice of the application must be given to the deputy attorney general of Canada, it was felt that the interests of the government department or authority administering the law that contains the time requirement or period of limitation will be adequately protected.
The bill provides that the granting of an order will be in the discretion of the judge. However, before he may exercise that discretion he must be satisfied on three points, namely,
(a)	that the applicant suffered loss or hardship as a result of the interruption of normal postal services;
(b)	that the applicant took such reasonable steps as were open to him to comply with the time requirement or period of limitation; and
(c)	that the application was made without undue delay.
Clause 3 also requires the judge to afford to any person who may be affected by any order that he may make an opportunity to be heard
Postal Services Interruption Relief Act or to make representations. Paragraph (d) of clause 3 provides that the judge may make an order waiving the time requirement or period of limitation and fixing a new one. Paragraph
(e)	of that clause provides, in effect, for the making of such further order as may be necessary to give full effect to an order made under paragraph (d). The provision in clause 3 that an order may be made subject to such conditions, if any, as to the judge seem just is intended to give flexibility that may be necessary in dealing with cases where third parties may be affected by the order.
[DOT] (4:40 p.m.)
Perhaps I should mention in closing that at the appropriate stage when the bill is before the committee I shall seek an amendment to the bill proposing the addition of one further clause of a procedural nature. It has been suggested to me, and I am inclined to think that the suggestion is a useful one, that it would be undesirable, where an application has been made to a particular judge, to require that all further proceedings consequent on the application must be taken by or before that judge. The proposed amendment would make it clear that any such further proceedings may be taken by or before any other judge of the court in the same way as though the application had been made initially to the court.

speakerposition: Minister of Forestry and Rural Development
maintopic: FUND FOR RURAL ECONOMIC DEVELOPMENT ACT
subtopic: AMENDMENT INCREASING AMOUNTS AVAILABLE UNDER AGREEMENTS WITH PROVINCES
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, royal assent was given on July 11 to Bill No. C-151 to provide for the establishment of a fund for the economic and social development of special rural development areas. The purpose of today's resolution and bill is to increase the fund from $50 million to $300 million-

When royal assent was given to establish the fund for rural economic development the legislation provided a special account in the consolidated revenue fund and the appropriate authority to enable the federal government and the provinces to join forces in concerted attacks on the problem of rural poverty. The approach was novel and significant in that it called for the joint development and
13514	COMMONS
Fund for Rural Economic Development Act implementation of comprehensive and coordinated programs for regions of acute rural poverty to raise substantially the standards of living of the residents of these areas as well as the economic and social opportunities open to them.
The fund was to be used to provide financial assistance beyond that normally available under the cost sharing provisions of the rural development agreement established under the ARDA legislation. More fundamentally, however, the legislation was designed to provide a means whereby federal and provincial agencies could work together to birng all available programs to bear jointly on depressed rural areas. The process leading to the signing of a federal-provincial agreement for the comprehensive development of special rural development areas involves several steps.
[DOT] (5:00 pjn.)
In the first place, development areas have to be identified. These are areas with readily apparent	problems of widespread and
severe low income, where the economic and social situation indicated little hope for improvement without special action and where there exists none the less a recognizable development potential. Economic and social studies are then undertaken to detail in depth the problems of the area and the appropriate remedies. These researchers can be carried out with substantial federal assistance under the Agricultural Rehabilitation and Development Act. Once the investigations are completed, the province and Canada can jointly draft a comprehensive development plan based on the studies and taking into account the attitudes of the local people as expressed through local committees. These integrated plans provide for a broad range of interrelated projects designed to increase income, raise the standards of living in the area and provide a better adjustment of resources and peoples. It should be stressed here that involvement of local people is built in throughout, both at the development and at the implementation stages.
When this legislation was introduced it was mentioned that studies were in progress in various areas of this country preparatory to the development of comprehensive plans. At that time, none of these studies had reached the point where a comprehensive plan had been finally developed. While we had every indication of substantial provincial interest, we could not yet be certain of the extent to which provinces would wish to participate in

DEBATES	February 27. 1367
large scale in integrated programs for specific areas. This uncertainty, as I will make clear later, has now been substantially removed.
At the time the bill was introduced into the house, we noted that studies were in progress in New Brunswick, Nova Scotia, Prince Edward Island, the interlake area of Manitoba and the lower St. Lawrence-Gaspe area of Quebec. Since then a new study has been initiated in Newfoundland. On September 20, 1966, Canada entered into two agreements with the province of New Brunswick under the terms of this legislation calling for comprehensive rural development plans for the northeastern and Mactaquac special rural development areas of that province. Northeastern New Brunswick, a region containing approximately 106,000 people, has a labour force of which approximately one-third are seriously underemployed or permanently unemployed. Incomes are just over $500 per capita, much less than half the Canadian average. Investments in social capital have lagged behind, especially in education. Thirty six per cent of the labour force have an education of grade 4 or less compared with 13 per cent for Canada, and only 17 per cent have reached grade 9 or higher compared with 33 per cent for Canada.
The main objective of the plan, as it was developed, is to provide for a major provincial commitment in education to enable the population to take advantage of new opportunities expected to become available in the area. There is provision for profound structural adjustments in the resource sector, to be accomplished by the province standing ready to buy land offered for sale to permit the rural people to benefit from technical and vocational training. There will be development work to assist fisheries; roads will be built to assist school consolidation and there may be some investment in recreation. A resettlement program is foreseen for those who voluntarily agree to move to larger centres to take advantage of new opportunities and social amenities.
The total development program calls for expenditures of $90 million. The federal contribution, including the cost of the manpower program, will exceed $62 million. The contribution from the fund for rural economic development is to exceed $31 million.
In the Mactaquac area, a smaller but similarly well balanced plan calls for a total com-itment of almost $21 million, with a contribution of more than $9 million from the fund.
February 27, 1967
The Mactaquac plan also foresees major retraining, resettlement and rehabilitation programs to go along with resource adjustment and development.
In signing agreements with the province of New Brunswick for two major comprehensive rural development programs, Canada has committed almost $41 million of the $50 million provided by the initial legislation which was passed by this house on May 12, 1966. The legislation provides that when an agreement is signed the funds must be encumbered. At the present time, however, the research phase in the interlake area of the province of Manitoba has been completed and the province and the officials of the Department of Forestry and Rural Development have drafted a proposed comprehensive development plan. This plan is now ready for final review by senior federal and provincial officials and, if accepted, will result in an agreement requiring a substantial commitment from the fund, possibly in excess of $25 million, although the total plan may cost about $65 million to $70 million.
In the initial debate in the house, many members suggested that $50 million was not enough to carry out the program that was outlined as the objective of the legislation. One hon. member commented that almost $2 billion would be required to develop the rural areas of Canada that are subject to chronic poverty conditions. At the time of discussion it was agreed that the initial $50 million would undoubtedly be insufficient to meet demands but that as yet there was some uncertainty as to the reception of this new concept in rural development by the provinces. We now have clear indications of provincial interest. The comprehensive plan for the interlake area may require at least $25 million from the fund.
Preliminary discussions are under way with the province of Quebec based on the report of the Bureau d'Amenagement de l'Est du Quebec and it is hoped that a mutually satisfactory strategy for the lower St. Law-renee-Gaspe area can culminate in an agreement with that province in the near future.
The investigations in Nova Scotia, Prince Edward Island, and Newfoundland are to be completed this year and agreements with those provinces might be concluded shortly thereafter. The totals of these programs, plus developments in certain areas of Ontario and the three remaining western provinces, will easily commit the balance of the $300 million.
The process through which plans can be developed has been determined and progress
Fund for Rural Economic Development Act has been rapid. We have good hopes that the provinces will now take advantage of the opportunities open to them to assist those rural regions that require special attention. We are confident that we can join together as partners to eliminate the conditions that have resulted in abject poverty for so many rural Canadians. The fund as it now stands is totally inadequate for that overriding purpose. Its enlargement to the proposed size should enable us to look forward more reasonably to the final elimination of rural poverty in Canada.
I hope that members of the committee will readily adopt this resolution.

speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, we on this
side of the house are not surprised at the minister coming once again with a request for additional funds to augment this program. We were dubious when the act was passed in May that $50 million would be adequate, particularly in view of the vast areas of this country devoted to agriculture. No matter how affluent agriculture may be in a province there are always some segments which, because of climatic conditions and geographical locations in relation to markets will suffer more than others to the detriment of the financial return to those engaged in agriculture in those areas.
[DOT] (5:10 p.m.)
When this legislation was introduced we in the official opposition took no exception to it and in fact were in accord with the principles outlined in it, but we had some reservations which we expressed at that time. One reservation was: Why was such an act necessary when one considers all the specific aids outlined in ARDA? Second, we asked how this act would be administered in conjunction with the ARDA program. We were particularly concerned about the joint action of the federal and provincial governments under this new legislation. It seemed to us that the provisions of Bill C-151 gave the federal government much more power to intrude into provincial jurisdiction than was necessary or had been granted under the provisions of ARDA.
We are not too adverse to the actions of the federal government in promoting the welfare of agriculture in the various provinces. I think farmers in general are not too particular where the aid comes from provided that the nature and substance of the aid are enough to really achieve something in depressed areas. But according to the explanation given by the minister today we see that the act allows a more concentrated effort

13516	COMMONS
Fund for Rural Economic Development Act in the way of federal aid in smaller, designated regional areas. It allows the more effective use of government funds to correct what is a very major problem in smaller areas to the degree that the financial return to the farmers or indeed the communities in those areas can be raised.
When this act was introduced by the minister he enumerated some of the things it was designed to do. In explaining the reasons for the act the minister stated that it certainly could not be used as disguised social welfare for any particular reason. He said it was not designed to provide work for the unemployed; this was not the major or principal consideration of the act. He said that the provisions of the act could not be used to support a rural economy whose resources could not carry it once the provisions of the act were withdrawn. If we understand the minister correctly, the basis of the act was to assess carefully the entire resources of an area and develop those regions wherein it was felt the resources could provide opportunities for the people to increase their potential and improve their standard of living. I think in the main this is what has been done.
I had intended to ask the minister what progress has been made in the interlake area of Manitoba, the Gaspe peninsula and northern New Brunswick, because these were the areas he designated in particular when introducing the bill. The information he provided in Hansard at that time gave no reason for mistaking the intentions of the measure. There was no reason for misinterpreting what the minister said on that occasion. He stated that these were areas in which something should certainly be done to improve the average income picture.
It seems that this act and the accompanying ARDA program are being used in a way which means that ARDA provides the funds for the exploratory, information gathering services that are so necessary before any comprehensive program can be undertaken. The minister indicated today that there are now other areas in Canada where initial investigations are taking place, and no doubt programs will be carefully worked out for these areas which will then approach the government for more funds.
We are not going to oppose the passage of this resolution calling for an increase in the fund from $50 million to $300 million. It is not a normal procedure after the introduction of a bill in this house to come back within a year and request an increase in the fund of

DEBATES	February 27, 1967
almost 600 per cent. That is the increase requested in the amount of money to be available. However, in view of the information given by the minister today and in view of the fears we expressed on the introduction of the bill, we feel that the increase is justified. Although $300 million is a tremendous amount of money, when we take into account the fact that it will be devoted to improving agriculture across Canada and realize how costly some of these projects must be if they are to improve the economy of a particular region, the fund is not excessive.
In his explanation today the minister placed a great deal of emphasis on the retraining and education being undertaken in these areas by the provinces. The very low educational standards in these regions is no reflection on the people there. The fact that they have these low standards is due to circumstances which have been forced upon them. We see this measure as the first step to bringing these areas out of their economic stagnation. We believe there is real hope in this program because with the facilities available today in the fields of science and applied technology we can do much to help these regions. In view of the fact that the government is taking the initiative at the federal-provincial level to make available these very essential tools to the people of these regions, we believe that at long last they have the opportunity to face the future with a great deal of hope.
We on this side of the house are not going to elaborate on this resolution because the act, as was indicated by the minister, was passed just last June and most of the arguments we put forth at that time still hold good as far as we are concerned. This is a new measure; it has just become active and a good deal of time will elapse before we are able to assess fairly and honestly how effective it has been. The only question that remains in my mind is where actual responsibility under the act ends and responsibility under ARDA comes into play. When we speak of an expenditure of $60 million or $80 million in one province under a single plan we certainly wonder whether a great deal of this work could not have been undertaken under ARDA. However, the minister will have an opportunity during the committee stage on the bill to elaborate on his explanation in this regard. That being so, I am prepared to allow the resolution to pass.

DEBATES	February 27, 1967
of planning and surveys in order to be efficiently developed. I happen to live in one of those areas, namely Abitibi, where considerable sums are required for the development of the immense natural resources of all kinds.
In a speech delivered to the two economic councils of the lower St. Lawrence region on October 23 last, the minister made the following statement:
The purpose of this program is to help the people living in rural areas adjust to the rapidly-changing economic situation, whether it be in agriculture or in other rural industries. I should like to point out to the minister -he may or may not be already aware of this-that Mr. Michel Sice, a consulting engineer, recently completed his report on a detailed survey of the Nottoway basin, in the Abitibi area. I have not had the opportunity to read or examine the report myself because it is still in the press, but I have read excerpts which appeared in our Val d'Or and Rouyn newspapers.
These excerpts show that this northwestern Quebec area is extremely rich, that is has been neglected to a considerable extent and that it should have been developed a long time ago.
With regard to agriculture, Mr. Sice noted that no real study of farming possibilities in this vast area had ever been made since Abitibi was first settled, 50 years ago. great possibilities in the pulp and paper industry. The report also adds that there is enough wood to supply 135 sawmills cutting one million board feet per year.

I wish to reinforce the argument of the New Democratic Party member who spoke of the need to bring the people into the program sought to be undertaken so they may participate personally. The hon. member's remarks apply particularly to the native population of our country. When I think of the various resources in my constituency and in nearby constituencies in Saskatchewan I think of the need to train and retrain people. This applies not only to the young but also to those in the older age groups. Training and retraining will enable such people to take a more active part in the producing capacity of our nation. Many of these people have skills of one kind or another and perhaps through the ARDA program they might develop these skills and produce things, thereby being able to live a better life than they live now. That should be possible without having to disrupt the way of life these people have chosen.
When one considers northern Saskatchewan, the frontier limits of our province, one immediately thinks of the wealth of tourist and recreational facilities and resources of the area. Nevertheless people there today are unemployed and are suffering greatly from poverty. These are the people who ought to be fitted into the development program. They have a place in this kind of development. I hope that the ARDA program in Saskatchewan and across Canada can give all such people their rightful place in our economic and social life. They ought to be brought into the program in such a way that other Canadians will have a renewed appreciation of the part that all can play. If that is done it will be good.

Since then as I mentioned at the resolution stage, we have proceeded with negotiations, with many of the provinces and we now know we will have to commit $250 million more in the next two years for rural development programs.
Some hon. members have asked, especially the hon. member for Kent (Ont.), why it is that the ARDA agreement is not sufficient to cover these rural development programs. There are many reasons for this, and I will enumerate a few. The first reason is that ARDA applies everywhere in Canada, that is, to any rural areas, while this fund applies only to certain specific regions where there is a concentration of low income families and where the income is usually half, or less than the average income for families across the nation.
The second reason for having this fund rather than an extension of the normal ARDA program is that under the ARDA program the provinces have an annual allotment. The third reason is that under the ARDA program and its agreements the federal government's contribution is limited to 50 per cent of the cost of any project. Under this fund for rural economic development the federal contribution can go up to 100 per cent of the cost of a project. Under the ARDA program we are committed to 5-year programs or projects. Under the fund for rural economic development we can commit the federal government's contribution for 10 years. Those are some of the reasons why we felt-and I explained this to the house-there was a necessity for this fund.
The hon. member for Medicine Hat said that he thought there was too much research and not enough implementation in respect of this program. The catalogue of the programs

of the ARDA administration has been distributed to all hon. members of the house and the public in general. This document deals with projects undertaken in 1962-65 and 1965-66. I do not want to have an argument with the hon. member, but in the province of British Columbia in the years 1963-65, the first term of the ARDA agreement, 35 projects were accepted for a total shareable cost of $3.7 million. If one looks at the list of projects he is surprised at the very limited number of research projects undertaken in the province. They are mostly concerned with the development of marginal land and the maintenance and improvement of agricultural production. There are projects listed to improve storage capacity for a reservoir, the reconstruction of a dam to increase productivity, to improve soils, and so on and so forth. There are listed very few research projects, at least in that province. If I look at the same document for the year 1965-66 I am amazed to see the extraordinary expansion in British Columbia. Shareable cost programs in British Columbia have increased in one year to $9.4 million, while in the first three years we committed only $3.7 million. So in that province, as in all other provinces, the ARDA program is picking up.
I will undertake to have the ARDA administration prepare for hon. members of the house and the general public an account of all the projects, by categories that is, soil, water conservation, research, rural development and so on so that hon. members will be able to judge for themselves exactly what has been done under this program. As hon. members know, the ARDA catalogue gives the description of each of the projects, but it does not classify them under various headings for the provinces. I think such a classification would be very useful. In this respect a good suggestion was made earlier. It would be useful because many people in this country are under the impression, and some people outside the house have made speeches to this effect, that ARDA is too much of a research program, and I think such a list would tend to prove that we have committed and spent very large sums of money on concrete projects, and not only on research. I do not think we have so far committed more than 10 per cent of our total funds on research; 90 per cent has been committed and the amount spent on various projects.

subtopic: IMPLEMENTATION OF VARIOUS AGREEMENTS RESPECTING DOUBLE TAXATION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the purpose of this bill, as its title indicates, is to give legislative effect to the recently signed income tax agreements with Trinidad and Tobago, Ireland, Norway, the United Kingdom and the United States. For convenience all these agreements have been incorporated into one bill, as had been done on previous occasions in recent years, and the bill has been divided into parts, each dealing with one agreement.
In substance the bill is similar to the bills implementing income tax agreements or supplementary income tax agreements between Canada and other countries that have been approved by the house since 1942. Canada now has in force 12 comprehensive income tax agreements with the United States of America, New Zealand, France, Sweden, Ireland, Denmark, West Germany, the Union of South Africa, the Netherlands, Australia, Finland and Japan.
The agreement with Trinidad and Tobago is new. The 1946 agreement with the United Kingdom was extended to Trinidad and Tobago when it was a colony and remained in force when it became an independent state; but that agreement was terminated. The new agreement, which reflects changes in the tax structure of Trinidad and Tobago, was negotiated immediately after the Common-wealth-Caribbean-Canada conference of last summer, and the minister was particularly pleased to be able to sign it together with the minister of finance of Trinidad and Tobago a few months later. Since the agreement will come into force as soon as each country has given legislative approval to it, and this has already been done in Trinidad and Tobago, we are hopeful that this agreement will come into force very shortly.
The agreement with Ireland replaces the existing comprehensive agreement with that country. The change of most significance to us is that Canada will have the right to impose a tax of 15 per cent on dividends paid to a parent company in Ireland by its subsidiary controlled company in Canada. Under the existing agreement the tax rate on such dividends is limited to 5 per cent.
The convention with Norway is new. A previous agreement signed in 1960 was not proceeded with because it provided for a

maximum 5 per cent rate on dividends from a subsidiary in one country to a parent in the other. The new convention provides for a maximum 15 per cent rate.
The agreement with the United Kingdom assimilates the provisions of the limited agreement that parliament approved last year and also contains provisions similar to those of other comprehensive agreements. The terms of the new agreement generally become effective from the dates when the 1946 Canada-United Kingdom agreement ceased to be effective, so that there is no hiatus between the provisions of the two agreements. The provisions of the new agreement relative to the new British taxes on corporations and capital gains become effective from the inception of these taxes. The agreement will enter into force when parliamentary approval has been given in both countries.
The supplementary convention with the United States of America is designed to overcome a tax avoidance device now being used by certain companies incorporated in Canada but not resident in Canada. The supplementary convention deals only with this change which was requested by the United States. The Canadian government has generally been postponing negotiations with other countries to be held with a view to revising existing tax agreements or entering into new agreements until after there has been an opportunity to examine fully the recommendations of the Royal Commission on Taxation. The other agreements dealt with in the bill now before the house are the culmination of negotiations held as a result of Canadian initiatives taken some years ago.

Consequently I think it is not necessary to delay the house for any length of time on second reading of the bill. Agreements of this type have been in existence for a considerable number of years as a means of avoiding double taxation, of preventing fiscal evasion and of endeavouring to promote international trade and commercial relations among the nations. They are highly complex and technical in nature, and I think it is in committee of the whole that the best examination can be given them. Indeed I doubt if there is anyone in the country who really fully understands the complexities of these agreements, except for that very dedicated public servant, Mr. F. R. Irwin, director

We believe that increased commercial relations would be greatly to the advantage of both countries.
The agreement with the United Kingdom is perhaps, that of greatest significance among the agreements which are in this bill. We will wish to know in committee just how the agreement which is now proposed integrates with the earlier agreements of June 5, 1946 and December 6, 1965.
The agreement with Norway is a new one which replaces an agreement which is perhaps the longest lived of all, since it has been in existence since May 4, 1929. The agreement with Ireland replaces one which has been in existence since October 28, 1954. The parliamentary secretary, sir, has told us that there are 12 agreements of this type and he has listed the countries with which we have such agreements.
