He said: Mr. Speaker, this bill to amend the Income Tax Act and to repeal the Canadian Vessel Construction Assistance Act is long and unfortunately somewhat complicated. Its amendments might be said to fall into four categories as follows:
1. Amendments to implement three paragraphs of the March, 1966 budget resolutions.
It will be recalled that the resolutions were approved by the committee of ways and means in June, 1966, and that all but three paragraphs in the resolutions were implemented in the income tax bill, Bill C-216, passed in July, 1966.
When Bill C-216 was before the committee last July I explained that it had not been possible to complete the drafting to cover all the proposals, but that it was the intention of the government to proceed with the remainder of the resolutions when the house resumed in the fall. The three paragraphs of the resolutions left to be implemented were: paragraph 11 dealing with deferred profit sharing plans, paragraph 12 dealing with transfers from pension plans or retiring allowances into a deferred profit sharing plan, and paragraph 13 dealing with supplementary unemployment benefit plans. The second category was the repeal of the Canadian Vessel Construction Assistance Act.
[DOT] (9:50 p.m.)
It may be recalled that when Bill No. C-216 was introduced last year it contained provisions dealing with the Canadian Vessel Construction Assistance Act. These provisions were withdrawn from Bill C-216 in order to give the shipping and shipbuilding industry time to study and make representations on the proposed changes. It was indicated that these provisions would be reintroduced in the autumn of 1966.

DEBATES	February 27. 1967
The third category was what I would call provincial abatements. It is necessary to change and extend the abatements of personal and corporation income taxes on income earned in a province in accordance with federal-provincial fiscal arrangements.
The fourth category is miscellaneous amendments, which included some changes to remove uncertainty and assist in the administration of the act.
This bill received first reading on December 21, 1966 but because some of the provisions are complicated it was thought desirable to allow a period of some weeks so that it could be thoroughly examined by all who are concerned. In this period the government has had the benefit of a number of submissions on particular parts of the bill and I shall have several amendments to place before the committee.
I shall be glad to provide comments and information as each subclause is called but since the bulk of the bill is made up of amendments dealing with deferred profit sharing plans and the Canadian Vessel Construction Assistance Act, and since these amendments are spread throughout the bill, it might be helpful if I gave a general outline at this stage of what is proposed in these two areas.
It will be noted that a substantial part of this bill deals with deferred profit sharing plans. The bulk of these amendments is contained in clauses 15 and 19 of the bill.
Hon. members will recall that the budget speech on March 29, 1966 announced that changes would be proposed to the Income Tax Act to prevent abuse of the provisions dealing with these plans. In that speech as reported on page 3385 of Hansard, I said:
In recent months there has been evidence of increasing abuse of the section of the act providing special tax treatment for deferred profit sharing plans. In 1960 and 1961 my predecessor, then the hon. member for Eglinton, with the worthiest of motives, introduced a section in the act to provide for these plans, which he described as an important piece of social legislation. Since then various businessmen and their professional advisers have exploited this well intended but vulnerable section in various ways. Essentially what happens in typical cases is that contributions of profits from a business, made deductible in computing income for tax purpose and held in a tax free fund, which were intended to benefit the employees of the business generally are being diverted to benefit a few key people, chief shareholders or their relatives or heirs.
Briefly, a deferred profit sharing plan is an arrangement under which payments, computed by reference to profits from a business, are
February 27, 1967

made by an employer into a trust on behalf of his employees. These payments, sometimes called contributions, are deductible for income tax purposes by the employer. The contributions are held by the trust for a period of years, very often until the employee retires. The earnings from investing these accumulating' funds by the trustee are not taxed in the hands of the trust. When the accumulated funds to the credit of an employee are paid to him, either as a retirement income or in a lump sum, these payments are taxable in his hands.
The two important tax features of these plans are that the employer obtains a deduction for amounts paid into the plan and the employee enjoys deferral of tax, often for many years, on the amounts eventually paid to him. In order to prevent abuse of these plans it has been found necessary to propose new rules dealing with several features of the plans including, first, vesting of the amounts allocated to each employee; second, reallocation of amounts when an employee leaves; third, investment of the funds held by a trustee, and, fourth, distribution of the accumulated funds.
It has also been necessary to impose penalty taxes to ensure that all the requirements are observed. Existing plans which are not now operating in accordance with the new rules will have to make changes to comply, but the amendments provide some time for these plans to make the necessary changes.
In drawing up these new rules there has been careful regard for the objectives of legitimate profit sharing plans. I think that most of the established plans that have been operated for the benefit of employees following the generally accepted principles of profit sharing will not be much affected by the new rules. Since the announcement last March that changes would be made we have had the benefit of a number of very helpful representations from persons who are familiar with profit sharing plans. In the two months that have elapsed since the proposed legislation was made public there has been a good opportunity for interested persons to examine the proposed changes in detail and again we have had the benefit of suggestions from those who are close to the operations of these plans. All the suggestions and representations received since December 19 have been helpful and they have been considered very carefully. It has not been found possible to accept all of these suggestions, but I shall have several amendments to place before the committee to
Income Tax Amendment improve the wording and to modify the application of the relevant clauses.
I shall be glad to give a more detailed explanation of the amendments as each clause and subclause is called, but by way of general outline I might point out that clause 16 lays down new requirements with which plans must comply in order to be accepted for registration. Clause 19 provides some rules of operation and imposes penalties for non-compliance.
Clause 15 would add five new paragraphs which describe conditions with which plans must comply if they are to be accepted for registration by the Minister of National Revenue (Mr. Benson) as deferred profit sharing plans. These are as follows: First, if the trustee under the plan is not a trust company there must be three trustees who shall be individuals. Second, all income received, all capital gains made and capital losses sustained by the trust must be allocated to beneficiaries under the plan within 90 days after the end of the year. Third, all amounts allocated or reallocated by a trustee under the plan to a beneficiary must vest in that beneficiary not later than five years after the year in which the amounts are allocated or reallocated unless the beneficiary has ceased to be an employee.
Fourth, the trustee must inform all new beneficiaries of their rights under the plan. Fifth, all amounts vested in an employee under a plan must become payable to that employee-or to his beneficiary or estate in the event of his death

promptly after the employee dies, leaves the employment or become age 71. However, the plan may provide that upon election of the employee all or part of the amounts payable to him may be paid in equal instalments over a period of 10 years or used to purchase an annuity.

Clause 19 will add a new Part II E to the act to impose certain penalty taxes where a trust governed by a deferred profit sharing plan does certain things. It also deals with returns and provides definitions. It will add new sections 105K to 105Q to the act.
The new section 105K will provide that every trust for a deferred profit sharing plan that acquires a non-qualified investment, or uses any property of the trust as security for a loan, shall pay a tax equal to the cost of the

non-qualified investment, or equal to the value of the property used as security for a loan, as the case may be. However, it is also provided that this tax shall be refunded when the trust disposes of a non-qualified investment or when a loan for which property has been pledged is renaid.
This new section also provides that a trust may use as much as 25 per cent of all amounts paid into it each year to pay premiums for life insurance of any kind without being deemed to have acquired a nonqualified investment. If the 25 per cent limit is exceeded the life insurance must be endowment type policies as described in the new section.
The new section 105L is intended to induce the trust for a plan to dispose of its nonqualified investments but it provides that this may be done gradually between now and the end of 1970. The proportion of non-qualified investments that must be disposed of in order to avoid a penalty tax are as follows: 20 per cent thereof by the end of 1967; 40 per cent thereof by the end of 1968; 60 per cent thereof by the end of 1969; 100 per cent thereof by the end of 1970.
Where a tax is imposed because nonqualified investments held on December 21, 1966 are not disposed of within the time limits, this tax will be refunded whenever disposal does take place provided the nonqualified investments are disposed of for not less than the full value placed on them on December 21, 1966. If there is some loss on disposal and the tax paid exceeds the loss there will be a partial refund of the tax.
A new section 105N will impose a tax when excessive amounts are re-allocated to remaining employees when other employees leave the plan. Since amounts paid into a plan and yearly earnings of the trust do not have to vest in members of the plan for five years there may be substantial amounts to be reallocated to remaining members of the plan when employees terminate their employment or otherwise leave the plan. The amounts that are forfeited by the terminating employees may be returned to the employer and included in his income for tax purposes or reallocated to remaining members of the plan. A tax of 50 per cent will be imposed on excessive re-allocations but the amount of a re-allocation to an employee will not be regarded as excessive unless it, plus the amounts paid into the plan by the employer on behalf of that employee, plus previous
February 27, 1967
tax-free re-allocations to that employee, exceed an amount equal to the number of years the employee has been in the plan times $2,000.
A new section 1050 requires a trustee for a plan to file returns for each year and a new section 105Q provides definitions including the definition of qualified investments for a trust under a plan. It should be borne in mind that the rules governing what shall be a qualified investment have been influenced by the need to prevent funds paid into a plan being returned to the employer as a loan that might never be repaid. The trust may buy the shares of the employer company where these shares are listed on a prescribed stock exchange in Canada and also in non-listed equity shares of the employer company where these shares meet certain tests. The right to invest in the shares of the employer company is an important part of the philosophy of some profit sharing plans since it is believed that this gives the employee a greater sense of participation in the business for which he works.
I apologize for this long and very complicated statement which departs somewhat from the rules governing debate on second reading, but without it I think it would have been very difficult for a debate to take place that would be relevant to this complicated change. I thank the house for its indulgence.

maintopic: TRADE-FAILURE TO MENTION LAKEHEAD CITIES IN ADVERTISING BROCHURE
TRADE-FAILURE TO MENTION LAKEHEAD CITIES IN ADVERTISING BROCHURE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, today I addressed the following question to the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Winters):
Has the attention of the minister been drawn to the elegant and presumably expensive brochure on Canada for distribution to the United States and. if so, did he take note that the cities of Fort William and Port Arthur were completely ignored? In fact, as far as this publication is concerned the Canadian lakehead does not exist.
In the minister's absence the Prime Minister (Mr. Pearson) took notice of the question and promised to bring it to the attention of

13548	COMMONS
Proceedings on Adjournment Motion the minister upon his return. However, I considered the matter of sufficient importance to ask for a debate on the adjournment motion. It seems inconceivable to me that the Canadian government travel bureau has permitted an elaborate publication to be circulated without showing complete access to Fort William and Port Arthur. I wonder whether those responsible for the printing of the booklet were really serious in producing a map which is supposed to show how Canada can be reached by train, plane and automobile, and leave out the whole of northwestern Ontario.
[DOT] (10:10 p.m.)
No Air Canada route to the cities of Fort William and Port Arthur is shown, nor is the North Central Airlines serving the lakehead mentioned. But the most glaring error is in the omission of the Canadian Pacific Railway passenger service, and of course the map leaves out even the international highway 61 from Duluth, Minnesota to the lakehead.
An appropriate editorial in the Fort William Times Journal bore the headlines: "It is in our own capital where education is needed", pointing out that there is no plausible excuse for such omissions.
The Northwestern Ontario Development Association, upon hearing of this unbelievable discovery, issued a news release condemning such an unseemly oversight, which may have the effect of drastically reducing the extent to which the lakehead area will share in the influx of tourists expected to be drawn to Canada by Expo.
The news bulletin of the association contains the following observations which are really a classic description of disappointment. It writes:
With Ontario's northwest thus relegated to the status of an almost inaccessible no-man's-land, it follows naturally that scant if any attention is given our region, either in the descriptive text of Canada's delights, or among the 140 colour photographs that cram this handsome publication.
The Ontario section, for instance, is dominated by a view of Niagara Falls. Other photos show Toronto's skyline, Upper Canada village, and an unidentified lakeside picture. The text, though brief, mentions tulip time at Ottawa, the Canadian National Exhibition at Toronto, the Royal Winter Fair at the same place, car racing at nearby Mosport, Highland Games at Maxville, Indian pageant at Brantford, Shakespearean Festival at Stratford and the flea market at Aberfoyle.
But what upsets the people of northwestern Ontario is the apparent disregard exhibited so often in the past by government agencies and

DEBATES	February 27, 1967
others, whose horizon apparently does not extend too far beyond the larger populated centres of Canada. I ask the minister to have the publication withdrawn and the proper correction made at the earliest possible moment.

speakeroldname: Hon. Jean-Luc Pepin (Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources):
speakerposition: Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources
maintopic: TRADE-FAILURE TO MENTION LAKEHEAD CITIES IN ADVERTISING BROCHURE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am speaking on behalf of the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Winters). I can well appreciate the disappointment of the hon. member for Fort William, and I sympathize with him in not seeing any reference to the cities of Fort William and Port Arthur in this publication. The reason is not that the lakehead cities were deliberately ignored but that a single booklet that skims over Canada's 10 provinces and two territories in 4,000 words of copy and 54 pages of photographs simply cannot do justice to every important community.
I am told that the travel bureau is now in the midst of giving thought to the production of an entirely new version of "Invitation to Canada" for 1968, and every consideration will be given to the inclusion of the cities of Fort William and Port Arthur.
However, after examining the first and second versions of other basic booklets distributed by the Department of Trade and Commerce I have realized that the department is really doing its best to give the lake-head the recognition it deserves. I have here a collection of booklets distributed by the department. One is entitled "Adventure along the Trans-Canada Highway". The red markers I have here are not to indicate the party to which the hon. member for Fort William belongs but simply to help me identify the references to the cities he represents so well. Another booklet is entitled "Canada Events 1967" and it indicates many events and festivities taking place in the lakehead this year. I have another pamphlet entitled, "Hay Fever, Canadian Havens From". It gives proper recognition to the climate of Fort William and Port Arthur. Then, I have a last pamphlet entitled, "Circle Tours from the Trans-Canada Highway". This one really gives Port Arthur and Fort William recognition with words like, "dynamic twin cities of the enormously important lakehead; a metropolis of 100,000 persons which offers a rare combination of scenic grandeur and industrial power." Fort William is referred to as, "the greatest grain port in the world," with the additional comment that "there are 25 grain

elevators which store annually over 100 million bushels of wheat." The pamphlet contains such phrases as, "see beautiful Boulevard Lake in the heart of Port Arthur". There is a reference to having "fun in Fort William's Chippewa Park", as well as a reference to a "miniature railway".

maintopic: CANADIAN NATIONAL RAILWAYS-EXPRESS DELIVERIES IN SAGUENAY-LAKE ST. JOHN AREAS
CANADIAN NATIONAL RAILWAYS-EXPRESS DELIVERIES IN SAGUENAY-LAKE ST. JOHN AREAS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, this afternoon I put the following question to the Minister of Transport (Mr. Pickersgill):
Is the minister aware that the C.N.R. officials have ordered the discontinuation of express services in the Saguenay, Lake St. John and, especially, Alma districts?
Many serious reasons prompted me to ask this question of the Minister of Transport. However, I shall limit myself to listing the main ones which I hope will succeed in getting the minister's sympathetic attention.
Last week end, I received many telephone calls from constituents who wanted to bring to my attention the fact that, in a very near future, they would be deprived of the express services now offered by the Canadian National Railways. Most of the people who complain are store owners, businessmen, industrialists living in Alma, my riding's major city with a population of approximately 25,000. It should be noted also that those businessmen extend their operations over 25 or 30 square miles.
Needless to say, Mr. Speaker, that our population feels that this decision is completely arbitrary and harmful to our region which has already been classified as economically weak. How can anyone imagine that such action will improve its economic and commercial situation? I doubt very much that it will.
I do not know, Mr. Speaker, if my suspicions are justified but until I get evidence to the contrary, I will find it very hard to get rid of them. I have good reason to believe that the government has chosen the Saguenay-Lake St. John area as a buffer zone where it can try out all kinds of experiments which most of the time go against the interests of our good people who have a right to expect fairer treatment from their government.
This means, Mr. Speaker, that our businessmen will have to spend time and money in order to pick up their goods in Jonquiere presumably; this is unacceptable, because I
Proceedings on Adjournment Motion feel the cost of delivery service which is presently available to them, is compensated to a large extent by express rates charged by the Canadian National Railways.
Of course, Mr. Speaker, economic reasons will be put forward; the point will be made that we must cut down on operating and administration expenses since the annual deficits of the national railway system, which is a crown corporation, must always be borne by the Canadian taxpayer. This reason does not stand up to examination, according to the comments and recommendations of the Auditor General of public accounts for Canada for the fiscal year ending March 31, 1966. We can reasonably say that the administrators are not particularly careful in their spending or, shall we say, do not hesitate to squander public funds.
Therefore, Mr. Speaker, on behalf of the riding I have the honour to represent in this house, and on behalf of all citizens whose rights have been violated by arbitrary deci-cisions of bureaucrats and well paid quill-drivers, I wish to voice vigorous protest against the way in which my constituents are being treated, and I urge the hon. minister to review this unfair policy, if there is still time.
[DOT] (10:20 p.m.)

TRANSPORT-SECOND FERRY BETWEEN NOVA SCOTIA AND NEW ENGLAND
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on Friday I raised or tried to raise with the Minister of Transport a matter concerning transportation of some importance to the economy of the maritime provinces. Your Honour ruled that I was a
13550	COMMONS
Proceedings on Adjournment Motion little verbose in my question and invited me to bring the matter up on the adjournment debate. I am now taking advantage of that advice. I regret that at this late hour the minister is not present, though I understand this. In view of his interest in and sympathy for all things for the good of the maritimes, I wish he were here. However, I trust that he has instructed his parliamentary secretary to give equally sympathetic consideration to the matter.
I should like to take this opportunity of calling the attention of the Minister of Transport to the need for supplementing the ferry service of the motor vessel Bluenose on the Bar Harbor, Maine-Yarmouth, Nova Scotia run during the coming summer months. As the minister and his parliamentary secretary undoubtedly know, the tourist business is of major economic importance to Nova Scotia and indeed to all maritime provinces. Tourist traffic demands have grown to such proportions that the Bluenose can no longer handle the traffic during the peak season. The necessity for making reservations for car space well in advance under the present congested summer traffic conditions tends to discourage potential traffic flow. Thus the actual over-demand for space is obscured, because people simply give up and do not visit the maritimes.
In addition to the tourist trade there is another function that the Bar Harbor ferry performs, that of carrying the truck transport of our fisheries exports. Since we are involved here with the freighting of a perishable commodity it is of fundamental importance that this particular traffic suffer no interruption or slow-down for the want of carrying capacity.
It has been the practice to give the Bluenose an annual overhaul in the winter. When she is laid up a substitute ferry of sorts has been provided. This year it was reported that a car ferry type of vessel, the Lief Erikson, suitable for the Bar Harbor summer service would be utilized during the Bluenose overhaul period. Owing to the accident to the ferry Cabot in Montreal harbour, the Lief Erikson was called in to take its place and was thus eliminated as a replacement for the Bluenose.
A small ship, inadequate as a summer supplement, was provided by the Department of Transport to render a minimum freight service at least. This emergency action was

DEBATES	February 27, 1967
much appreciated. On the assumption that the Cabot will be back in commission by next June, I urge the minister to assign her to fill the aching void next summer-the aching void I have called to his attention.
In pressing the project I have been discussing, and to emphasize the dollars and cents practicality of it, I draw attention to the fact that during the period January 1, 1965, to December 31,	1965, the ferry Bluenose
showed an operating profit of some $19,000.
Finally, sir, while reminding the minister again that the ferry service to Bar Harbor is basic to the trade in tourists and fish of Nova Scotia, Prince Edward Island and Newfoundland-a pipe line as it were-I venture the hope that the minister will not allow this pipe line to become intolerably constricted.

Mr. Speaker, I wish to assure the hon. member that the minister's absence is not an indication that he does not consider this a most important matter. He is on important business elsewhere this evening. I have information supplied by the department, and I am sure the hon. member is aware of some of that information that I have this evening.
The Bluenose service was set up originally as a result of a co-operative arrangement between the federal government and the provincial government, under which each assumed a portion of the capital cost involved at the outset. Two or three years ago the federal government made a special study and forecast which indicated that the longer term traffic growth between southern Nova Scotia and New England would, in due course, justify additional service.
Around that time, and arising out of this, the provincial government suggested that a special consultant be employed to report more specifically on the need for an additional ferry, and the terminals which should be used. The federal government agreed to share in the costs of this study. The study itself was completed last year-in the first half of 1966-and made available to the province, and through the province to the federal government. This indicated there was need for eventual development of additional service. Several alternative routes were studied, with particular attention being given to the desirability of a Bay of Fundy routing.
